Synergistic Pd/Cu-Catalyzed Cascade Reactions

ABSTRACT: Herein, we describe a method in the one-pot synthesis of cyclic 1,3-enynes and allenynes from alkynyl-allenyl cross-
coupling and cascade reactions of vinylidenecyclopropane-diesters (VDCP-diesters) with a large number of unactivated terminal
alkynes for the formation of a C(sp
2
)−C(sp) bond under palladium/copper dual catalysis and assisted by base Cs
2
CO
3
and NEt
3
with distinctly different Brønsted basicity and Lewis basicity. This developed divergent transformation proceeds through a key rapid
transmetalation and the subsequent intramolecular cyclization process regulated by cesium effect. Our investigations found that
these reactions can occur under mild conditions and have a broad substrate scope with a wide range of functional groups via a
zwitterionic palladium species, affording the corresponding desired products in moderate to good yields. Further synthetic
transformations show the application value of this protocol. Plausible reaction mechanisms have also been proposed on the basis of
control, deuterium labeling experiments, and density functional theory calculations.
KEYWORDS: C(sp
2
)−C(sp) cross-coupling, palladium/copper dual catalysis, cesium effect, divergent synthesis,
zwitterionic palladium species
■
INTRODUCTION
As the precursors and high value-added derivatives of allenes,
cyclic 1,3-enynes and allenynes serve as key components in a
variety of functional materials and act as unique reactive
intermediates in organic synthesis.
1−12
A large number of
literature have reported that these compounds not only possess
important physiological and pharmacological activities but also
have plentiful reactivities for the synthesis of natural products
and drug-like molecules (Scheme 1A).
1,13−20
However, the
lack of efficient and versatile synthetic methods has
significantly hindered their broader application in synthetic
chemistry and biological studies. Consequently, considerable
efforts have been devoted to exploring novel methodologies for
their efficient syntheses over the past few decades. The current
synthesis of cyclic 1,3-enynes and allenynes typically involves
palladium-catalyzed cross-coupling reactions to construct the
new C(sp
2
)-C(sp) bond, where terminal alkynes or alkynyl
organometallic reagents are used to react with alkenyl or allenic
halides.
21−27
Nevertheless, this process typically necessitates
the introduction of appropriate leaving groups onto alkenyl,
allenyl, or propargyl moieties and does not ensure compati-
bility with other functional groups (Scheme 1B). Therefore,
upon synthesizing cyclic 1,3-enynes and allenynes with unique
structures, it remains essential to identify appropriate
alternative methods.
Nonetheless, several challenges remain to be resolved in the
formulation of a comprehensive strategy for their synthetic
methods. For example, these methods should feature rapid
synthesis, a broad substrate scope, mild reaction conditions,
high reaction yields, and excellent atom economy. In this
research aspect, Ma,

Liu,

Han and Shen,

excellent work on the development of elegant strategies for the
synthesis of allenynes and the related substances, respectively.
However, the synthetic approaches reported to date have yet
to achieve the synthesis of 1,1-disubstituted allenynes that can

On the other hand, compared to reactions involving π-allyl

38,39

It can be noted that this zwitterionic propargyl palladium
intermediate usually exists in three forms, including η

51,52
In the studies reported to date, the
reaction methods employed to capture these active inter-
mediates have predominantly been dipolar cycloaddition and
nucleophilic addition. Our group has published several studies
based on vinylidenecyclopropane-diesters (VDCP-diesters) as
a zwitterionic allenyl palladium dipolar precursor in recent
years (Scheme 1C(a)).
53−58
As an interesting special class of
allenic derivatives, VDCP-diesters are the molecules with high
tension but are relatively stable at room temperature (Scheme
1C(a)).
59
Additionally, Lu, Xiao, Zhang, and their co-workers
have developed a series of propargyl palladium dipolar
intermediates and reported a higher-order dipolar cyclo-
addition strategy in 2024 (Scheme 1C(b)).
60
On the basis of these previous works, we attempted to carry
out further investigation on the development of a new reaction
mode of zwitterionic allenyl palladium intermediates different
from existing reaction modes. In this paper, we wish to report a
Pd/Cu bimetallic synergistic catalysis and cesium effect-
mediated/controlled cascade reactions based on VDCP-
diesters, which induced a divergent synthetic method of cyclic
1,3-enynes and allenynes that are obtained under the
regulation of different bases (Scheme 1D). In contrast to the
conventional reaction method, this reaction achieves in situ
capture of the zwitterionic allenyl palladium species via a rapid
transmetalation process, thereby obtaining the crucial inter-
mediates. This protocol not only realizes a newly controllable
transformation of strained small ring connected allenes to the
other key intermediates
61−63
but also provides a reference idea
for the efficient synthesis of conjugated moiety.

To initiate our studies, we started with a model reaction using
vinylidenecyclopropane-diethyl ester 1a (1.0 equiv) and
phenylacetylene 2a (1.5 equiv) as the coupling partners to
optimize the reaction conditions. A bimetallic catalyst system
consisting of the Pd(0) complex Pd(PPh

the reaction would not occur at all, and the equivalent of base

Gratifyingly, the corresponding allenyne product 4aa was

screened, and among these copper salts used, CuI was

On the basis of the above optimized conditions for this Pd/
Cu-cocatalyzed divergent synthetic protocol, the substrate
scope was investigated, and the results are displayed in
Schemes 2 and 3.
To begin with these investigations under standard
conditions A, we studied the application scope of unactivated
terminal alkyne substrates in the reaction with VDCP-diester
1a. For phenylacetylene derivatives with substituents on the
benzene ring, cyclic 1,3-enyne products 3ab−3am can be
obtained in moderate to excellent yields. However, groups with
electron-withdrawing effects often had higher yields than those
of substrates with electron donors (3ab−3af, 3ah, and 3ai
compared with 3aj−3al). This may be attributed to the fact
that cyclization is an intramolecular nucleophilic addition
process. The substituents at the para-position of the benzene
ring influence the electron cloud density of the allenic carbon−
carbon double bond through the extensive conjugated system,
and the reactivity of relatively electron-deficient allenes is
higher. A special case of para-bromine-substituted phenyl-
acetylene (2g), which had a yield of only 46%, was probably
due to the side effects of other C−C cross-couplings under the
reaction conditions. In addition, the electronic effects of ortho-
chlorine-substituted and para-chlorine-substituted phenylace-
tylene are similar, and their yields (97%, 96%) were not much
different. In addition to the benzene ring, other aromatic rings
such as naphthalene and phenanthrene-derived terminal yne
substrates are also well adapted to this transformation reaction,
and the corresponding target products 3an−3ap can be
obtained in yields of 58%−61%. If the conjugated system of
the substrate is extended with a carbon−carbon double bond
(2q) or triple bond (2r) between the aromatic ring and the
terminal alkyne, the reactions can still occur relatively well,
affording products 3aq and 3ar in yields of 73% and 71%,
respectively. In addition, the aromatic heterocycle-derived
terminal alkyne substrates, including pyridine and thiophene
(2s−2w), are also compatible with this Pd/Cu bimetallic
synergistic catalytic system, the relative position of the
heteroatoms on the ring has little effect on the yield of the
reaction, and the target products 3as−3aw can be obtained in
the yields of 79%−86%. One interesting case has also been
tested, in which substrate 2x is commonly used as a copper-
catalyzed propargylic substitution reaction. Despite this
competing reaction, we found that the cyclic 1,3-enyne
product 3ax was still obtained as the main product under
standard conditions A in 67% isolated yield. Several alkyl-
substituted terminal alkyne substrates have also been tried,
including alkyne substrate (2y), TMS (2z) or TBS-protected
(2aa) alkynes, acetal (2ab), alkyl ether (2ac), alkyl aryl ether
(2ad), Boc-protected piperidine ring (2ae), ethyl (2af), and
cyclohexyl (2ag), all of which have been shown to be suitable
for this conversion reaction. The yields of the desired products
ranged from 42% to 76% (3ay−3aag), reflecting the wide
applicability of the reaction substrates.
Subsequently, we set out to investigate a wide range of
VDCP-diesters upon reacting with 2a under the standard
conditions A. Compared to VDCP-diester 1a, reaction of 1b
with a dimethyl ester group with 2a also proceeded smoothly,
affording the corresponding product 3ba in 84% yield.
Increasing the steric hindrance of ester groups, such as
VDCP-diester 1c bearing a diisopropyl ester group and VDCP-
diester 1d with dibenzyl esters, the corresponding products 3ca
and 3da were obtained in 70% and 59% yields, respectively,
suggesting that the steric effect of VDCP-diesters indeed has
some impact on the reaction outcome. If there is an isopropyl
substituent on the three-membered ring of VDCP (1e), the
reaction was specific to obtain an allenyne-type product 4ea,
probably due to the substituent on the side not being
conducive to the intramolecular ring closing process. For the
VDCP-diester with ethyl substitution at the terminal of the
allene moiety, the reaction can also proceed smoothly to obtain
the corresponding cyclic 1,3-enyne product 3fa in 85% yield;
when the ethyl group here is replaced with a phenyl group, the
target product 3ga cannot be obtained. Finally, we obtained
product 3db in 72% yield using substrates 1d and 2b, and the
structure of the product was also confirmed by an X-ray single-
crystal diffractometer.
Next, the scope of the cross-coupling reaction under the
optimal standard conditions B for allenyne-type products was
also investigated. Similarly, we first looked at the scope of
application of terminal alkyne substrates on the basis of
reactions with 1a and found that varying different substituents
at the para- and ortho-position on the benzene ring afforded
the corresponding products 4ab−4am in 44−92% yields.
However, the yield was also lower when the para-position was
bromine substituted, giving 4ag in only a 44% yield. Moreover,
larger conjugated systems, including naphthalene (2an & 2ao),
phenanthrene (2ap), and inserted carbon−carbon double
bond (2aq) or carbon−carbon triple bond (2ar), were also
tolerated in this reaction, which can also harvest the target
products 4an−4ar in 57%−72% yields. The pyridine ring and
thiophene ring substituted at different positions can also be
well adapted to the reaction conditions, and the corresponding
target products 4as−4aw (except 4at) can be obtained in
yields of 60% to 79%, respectively. It is important to note that
when 3-ethynylpyridine 2t was used as the coupling
component, the reaction resulted in a mixture of allenyne
4at and 1,4-diyne 4at′ (ca. 1.8:1.0, 77% total yield), and it is
speculated that 4at′ was formed because of the presence of the
isomerization of zwitterionic η
1
-(allenyl)palladium species into
η

S21 on page S29 in the Supporting Information). In addition,
the terminal alkynes substituted by the alkyl and silyl protective

reaction, and the corresponding target products 4ax−4aag can
be obtained in 47% to 77% yields.
In addition, changing the ester groups in VDCP-diesters 1
from a dimethyl ester group to a diisopropyl ester group to
react with 2a also smoothly delivered the corresponding
allenyne products 4ba−4ca in 60% to 82% yields. In particular,
when using the dibenzyl ester group-substituted VDCP

To illustrate the synthetic utility of this Pd/Cu dual-
catalyzed cross-coupling synthesis of vinylidenecyclopropane-
diesters, gram-scale reactions have been conducted. We used
VDCP-diester 1a (1.01 g, 4.8 mmol) and phenylacetylene 2a
(0.74 g, 7.2 mmol) under the two different standard conditions
A and B. The results show that the scale-up syntheses were
performed successfully to verify the utility of the reaction,
affording the corresponding products 3aa or 4aa in 81% and
82% yields, respectively (Scheme 4A).
Moreover, some further transformations of the obtained
products 3aa and 4aa have also been investigated (Scheme
4B). On the one hand, cyclic 1,3-enyne 3aa can achieve highly
selective epoxidation of the olefinic fraction upon treating with
3-chloroperoxybenzoic acid (m-CPBA) and furnish the epoxy
compound 5 in 77% yield. Besides, one of the two ester groups
in substrate 3aa can be efficiently removed at a high
temperature to gain the single product 6 with 73% yield. In
addition, the diethyl ester group can be converted into other
substituents such as primary amide 7, which is generally
difficult to achieve in the synthesis of the corresponding VDCP
substrate. On the other hand, for the allenyne 4aa, it can
undergo an intramolecular nucleophilic addition reaction to
close the ring under the catalysis of Au(I) metal salt, with a
yield of 83% to generate the product 3aa under mild reaction
conditions. An α-alkylation reaction can be carried out under
the action of strong base NaH, and the methylated product 8
can be obtained in 87% yield when MeI was used as an
electrophile.
In order to validate the reaction mechanism, we performed a
series of mechanistic experiments. We initially attempted to
explore the potential active intermediates present in the
reaction system. An excess of copper phenylacetylene SI-12
was employed in lieu of the catalytic amount of cuprous iodide,
and phenylacetylene was not added simultaneously. The
reactions were conducted under standard conditions A or B,
respectively (Scheme S8a,b in the Supporting Information);
however, they did not occur successfully. It was hypothesized
that this feeding manner inhibited the hydrogen transfer
process in the reaction. To further validate our speculation,
CsHCO
3
was used to replace Cs
2
CO
3
under standard
conditions A, and NEt
3
·HCl was used to replace NEt
3
under
standard conditions B. Through the additional introduction of
a proton source, it was confirmed that the reaction could
proceed smoothly, enabling the specific acquisition of the
corresponding products with yields of 18% and 11%,
respectively (Scheme S8c,d in the Supporting Information).
This result suggests that the proton transfer process during the
reaction is essential. The low yield might be attributed to
excessive proton source leading to the occurrence of other side
reactions and reducing the alkalinity of the reaction system.
To further elucidate the proton transfer pathway in the
reaction, deuterium incorporation experiments were subse-
quently conducted under standard conditions A and B, as
illustrated in Scheme S10 in the Supporting Information. The
use of homemade deuterated 2a-d as a substrate to react with
VDCP-diester 1a afforded 3aa-d in 83% yield along with 29%
deuteration and 4aa-d in 80% yield along with 26%
deuteration, respectively. The low deuterium substitution
ratio in the products can be attributed to the rapid
hydrogen−deuterium exchange that occurs between the
deuterated protons and the ambient water or moisture that
is difficult to completely remove from the reaction system.
Based on the previous studies, we speculate that there is a
coordination of Cu and a carbon−carbon triple bond in
phenylacetylene in the reaction, and the hydrogen atom at the
terminal position of phenylacetylene is deprotonated by the
base in the system after activation and then enters into the
product molecule through the subsequent transformation
process.

CONCLUSION
In summary, a Pd/Cu dual catalysis and Cs
2
CO
3
and NEt
3
-
mediated divergent synthesis of terminal alkynes with
zwitterionic palladium intermediates generated from VDCP-
diesters has been developed, obtaining two different
structurally diverse products, cyclic 1,3-enynes and allenynes,
with high research value. This divergent synthesis can gain
various aromatic or alkyl structure substitution products in
moderate to good isolated yields with good functional group
compatibility. On the basis of our experimental results as well
as DFT calculations, palladium is vitally important to the
formation of key intermediate zwitterionic palladium species,
and copper concurrently performs the functions of trans-
metalation and catalytic cyclization in the reaction, which
significantly ameliorated the issue of low cyclization yield
under the condition of single copper catalysis to a considerable
extent, thereby manifesting the superiority of synergistic
catalysis in one-pot. The employed bases such as cesium
carbonate and triethylamine, which function as proton transfer
shuttles, lead to divergent synthetic outcomes in the reaction
due to their distinctly different Brønsted basicity and Lewis
basicity. Moreover, the cesium effect is of vital significance for
the smooth occurrence of the induced cascade reaction. In the
whole process, the two different bases promote the trans-
metalation process and regulates the intramolecular nucleo-
philic addition by interacting with copper. In addition, as the
key intermediates of chiral transformation and synthesis, cyclic
1,3-enynes and allenynes themselves have been reported to
undergo interesting reactions as multifunctional synthons.
Further research based on the products of this divergent cross-
coupling reaction for the synthesis of chiral biologically active
molecules are undergoing in our laboratory now. Moreover,
considering that the chirality of the compound has attracted
considerable attention, an asymmetric version of these
reactions is also underway.
